maverick.gloss: Maverick refers to a person who refuses to follow the customs or rules of a group; in other words, a nonconformist.
maverick.example: Ayo has always been a bit of a maverick in the fashion world, inventing new trends rather than following them.

demigirl.gloss: ( neologism ) One who identifies as partially, but not completely, female .

apprenticeship.gloss: The condition of, or the time served by, an apprentice .

glamour.gloss: ( uncountable ) Originally, enchantment ; magic charm ; especially, the effect of a spell that causes one to see objects in a form that differs from reality, typically to make filthy, ugly, or repulsive things seem beauteous .

docking.gloss: ( nautical ) The securing of a vessel to the quayside with cables .

plurality.gloss: ( uncountable ) The state of being plural .

scacchic.gloss: ( rare ) Of or relating to chess .

deprecate.gloss: ( transitive ) To express disapproval of, protest or plead against.

boston-marriage.gloss: ( historical ) A long-term monogamous relationship between two unmarried women, especially in New England between the 18th and early 20th centuries.

union.gloss: ( countable ) The act of uniting or joining two or more things into one.

It is used especially for people who travel in a circuit for their profession. // Being an itinerant musician gave her the opportunity to see the wonders of the world with her own eye

life-car.gloss: ( historical ) A watertight boat or box , travelling on a line from a wrecked vessel to the shore , used to haul people through the waves in a rescue.

Vituperate can also mean "to use harsh condemnatory language." // They were vituperated for betraying their friends. first-strike.gloss: ( military ) An attack (typically nuclear ) launched without warning in the absence of a prior attack by one's opponent , with the intention of destroying the opponent's ability to retaliate .

aerie.gloss: Merriam-Webster's Word of the Day for July 26, 2026 is: aerie  \AIR-ee\   noun Aerie refers to the nest of a bird (such as an eagle or hawk) built high up on a cliff or on the top of a mountain. It can also be used for a room or building built high up so that people inside can see things happening below them. // From the lighthouse's aerie tourists can get a bird's-eye view of the rocky coa

parochial.gloss:  adjective Parochial is a formal word that is usually used in a disapproving way to describe something that is limited in range or scope, as to a narrow region or area.
parochial.example: For some, college can be an expansive experience that lifts them out of a parochial mindset.

kludge.gloss:  noun A kludge is a haphazard or makeshift solution to a problem and especially to a computer or programming problem.
kludge.example: Andy knocked out a hasty kludge to circumvent the glitch until a more robust solution could be developed.

inveigle.gloss:  verb To inveigle someone is to persuade them in a clever or deceptive way to do something. Inveigle can also mean “to get something in a clever or deceptive way.”
inveigle.example: According to rumors, the company inveigled employees into signing the agreement. // Their attempts to inveigle the information from her were, eventually, fruitful.

sultry.gloss:  adjective Sultry means “very hot and humid” when it describes such things as seasons, days, and weather. When it describes things humans do and possess—voices, poses, looks, and the like—it means “exciting or capable of exciting strong sexual desire.”
sultry.example: The restaurant's rooftop deck is the place to be on sultry summer nights.

comely.gloss:  adjective Comely is an adjective with an old-fashioned and literary feel that describes someone or something that has a pleasing appearance, or that is pretty or attractive.
comely.example: The newlyweds make quite a comely couple.

spindrift.gloss:  noun Spindrift refers to spray blown from waves during a gale or to fine wind-borne snow or sand.
spindrift.example: Our whale-watching cruise was a whirlwind of flukes, fins, and clinging to the handrails amid the waves and salty blasts of spindrift.

highfalutin.gloss:  adjective Something or someone described as highfalutin seems, or is trying to seem, great or important.
highfalutin.example: The authors’ research may have been impressive, but their paper was full of highfalutin jargon that ultimately obscured what they intended to say.

mitigate.gloss:  verb To mitigate something is to make it less severe, harmful, or painful.
mitigate.example: One way we can mitigate the impact the construction project will have on residents is to commit to completing it in the allotted time.

lan.gloss:  noun Élan refers to energy and enthusiasm.
lan.example: The dancers performed with great style and élan; we were exhausted just watching them.

colloquial.gloss:  adjective Colloquial is used with words like term and word and expression to describe language that is used in familiar and informal conversation.
colloquial.example: The author can switch from formal academic language to a charmingly colloquial style, depending on the audience and subject of her writing.

torpor.gloss:  noun Torpor is a formal word for a state of inactivity and sluggishness. It can also be used, especially in the context of hibernating and estivating animals, to refer to a state of lowered physiological activity.
torpor.example: The magazine offers lots of ideas for activities designed to shake off the torpor of a rainy day.

invidious.gloss:  adjective Invidious is a formal word used to describe things that are unpleasant and likely to cause bad feelings in other people. Such bad feelings may include resentment, discontent, animosity, or envy.
invidious.example: Psychologists caution against drawing invidious comparisons between other people’s lives as portrayed on social media and one’s own.

nurture.gloss:  verb Nurture is most often used to mean “to help someone or something grow, develop, or succeed.” It can also mean “to take care of someone or something that is growing or developing by providing food, protection, a place to live, etc.,” or “to hold something, such as an idea or strong feeling, in your mind for a long time.”
nurture.example: Art teachers nurture their students’ creativity. // She nurtured a secret ambition to be a professional singer.

anecdote.gloss:  noun An anecdote is a short narrative about an interesting, funny, or biographical incident.
anecdote.example: Dinner with our uncles means lots of anecdotes involving the mischief they got into as kids.

pedagogical.gloss:  adjective Pedagogical is a formal word used to describe things that are of or related to teachers or education.
pedagogical.example: The new professor is known for particularly engaging pedagogical methods.

baptism-of-fire.gloss:  noun A baptism of fire (or baptism by fire, as it is sometimes referred to in the U.S.) is an introductory or initial experience that is a severe ordeal. In military contexts, baptism of fire specifically refers to a soldier's first exposure to enemy fire.
baptism-of-fire.example: The newly recruited player faced a baptism of fire as the team went head to head with their greatest rival.

gnomic.gloss:  adjective Gnomic is a formal word that describes something cryptically said or written in few words.
gnomic.example: The painter is notorious for offering terse, gnomic responses to questions about her work that leave interviewers and critics scratching their heads.

salvo.gloss:  noun In military contexts, salvo refers to various actions involving discharge or release of bombs, rockets, artillery, etc., as well to the bombs or projectiles released in such an action. In general use, salvo is usually used to refer to a strong or sudden verbal attack, but it can also refer to a sudden occurrence of applause, laughter, etc., from many people.
salvo.example: The troops were driven back by a salvo of cannon fire. // The editorial's opening salvo was a list of grievances against the mayor's policies. // The conclusion of her performance was answered with a salvo of cheers and applause.

vacuous.gloss:  adjective Vacuous is a formal word indicating a lack of thought, intelligence, or substance.
vacuous.example: Despite a lengthy advertising campaign pitching the film as a masterwork, critics ultimately assailed it as dull and filled with self-important characters spouting vacuous platitudes.

circumscribe.gloss:  verb To circumscribe something is to limit its range or activity.
circumscribe.example: The president’s decision-making power was carefully circumscribed by the company’s board.

zeugma.gloss:  noun Zeugma refers to wordplay in which a single word relates to other words in such a way that it means something different in each case, as in “building a boat and a reputation” and “open a book along with your mind.”
zeugma.example: A clever use of zeugma was demonstrated by Groucho Marx’s character Rufus T. Firefly in Duck Soup (1933): “You can leave in a taxi. If you can’t get a taxi, you can leave in a huff. If that’s too soon, you can leave in a minute and a huff.”

lackadaisical.gloss:  adjective Something or someone described as lackadaisical is lacking in interest, enthusiasm, or zest.
lackadaisical.example: Feeling particularly lackadaisical in the summer heat, they lazily tossed a ball back and forth.

oxymoron.gloss:  noun An oxymoron is a combination of words that have opposite or very different meanings, such as "cruel kindness" or "open secret." In broader usage, oxymoron can also refer to something (such as a concept) that is made up of contradictory or incongruous elements.
oxymoron.example: Some of Shakespeare's most famous plays are filled with oxymorons such as "loving hate" and "tragical mirth."

balmy.gloss:  adjective Balmy is an adjective that is often used to describe weather that is warm, calm, and pleasant. It can also be used to describe someone or something (such as an idea) that is foolish or irrational.
balmy.example: After a long, eight-hour drive, we were rewarded with a mild, balmy evening at our vacation spot on the shores of Lake Erie. // Despite being a devout Green Bay fan, she finds the idea of attending games in head-to-toe yellow and green body paint to be a bit balmy.

divulge.gloss:  verb To divulge something, especially secret or private information, is to make it known.
divulge.example: Rather than divulge the baby name we’ve chosen, we’re waiting till the little one arrives to make introductions.

rigmarole.gloss:  noun Rigmarole refers to a long, complicated, and annoying process, description, etc.
rigmarole.example: We went through the rigmarole of installing, registering, and activating the software before we found out it wouldn’t work.

august.gloss:  adjective The word august, which is pronounced with the accent on "gust," describes someone or something marked by majestic dignity or grandeur.
august.example: We toured the old mansion's august halls and expansive grounds.

prowess.gloss:  noun Prowess refers to someone’s great ability, skill, or talent for something specified, as in “the pop star's vocal prowess” or “a lawyer of great prowess.”
prowess.example: Already a proven virtuoso on guitar, she extends her considerable instrumental prowess to the piano throughout her new album as well.

expeditious.gloss:  adjective Expeditious is a formal word that is used to describe someone acting in a quick and efficient way, or something done in such a manner.
expeditious.example: Both sides hoped for an expeditious resolution of the dispute.

tilde.gloss:  noun Tilde refers to the mark ~ placed especially over the letter n (as in the Spanish señor, meaning "sir") to denote the sound \nʸ\, or over vowels (as in the Portuguese irmã, meaning "sister") to indicate nasality. When a tilde appears as an independent character, it usually means "approximately" (as in "we'll be there in ~ 30 minutes").
tilde.example: A familiar example of the tilde appears in the name of Brazil's capital city, São Paulo.

devolve.gloss:  verb To devolve is to gradually go from an advanced state to a less advanced state, or to pass something, such as responsibility or power, from one person or group to another at a lower level of authority.
devolve.example: Somehow the debate devolved into a petty competition to see who could get more applause. // Community leaders hope that the new government will devolve more power to the community itself.

southpaw.gloss:  noun Southpaw is an informal word for someone who is left-handed. It is especially used for a left-handed baseball pitcher or boxer.
southpaw.example: The team’s new pitcher is a southpaw with a wicked knuckleball.

cogent.gloss:  adjective Cogent is a formal word that describes something that is very clear and easy for the mind to accept and believe. It is used as a synonym of convincing.
cogent.example: At the town meeting, citizens presented many cogent arguments in support of building a new senior center.

kith.gloss:  noun Kith is an old-fashioned term that refers to familiar friends, neighbors, or relatives. It is often used in the phrase “kith and kin,” which means “friends and relatives.”
kith.example: Spending time with kith and kin at the end of the summer is the highlight of our year.

illustrious.gloss:  adjective Illustrious describes a person or deed that is highly admired and respected.
illustrious.example: During the ceremony, the illustrious star of stage and screen was presented with a lifetime achievement award.

gumption.gloss:  noun Gumption refers to courage and confidence.
gumption.example: It took a lot of gumption to speak up for yourself like that.

conscientious.gloss:  adjective Conscientious describes someone who is concerned with doing things correctly. It can be used as a synonym for both meticulous and careful.
conscientious.example: She has always been a conscientious worker committed to painstaking research.

dissonant.gloss:  adjective Dissonant typically describes music that is not in harmony, or sounds and notes that clash. In non-music contexts, dissonant describes things that clash by not being in agreement or by not fitting well together.
dissonant.example: The guitarist struck a dissonant chord. // The retrospective provided a sometimes dissonant journey through the artist's decades of work.

recalcitrant.gloss:  adjective Recalcitrant is a formal word typically used to describe someone who stubbornly refuses to obey rules or orders. Recalcitrant can also describe something that is difficult to manage or operate.
recalcitrant.example: The magazine, aimed at parents and caregivers of young children, will include the latest in child development science as well as practical information, like tricks for persuading even the most recalcitrant toddler to cooperate.

apiary.gloss:  noun Apiary refers to a place where bees are kept, and especially a collection of hives or colonies of bees kept for their honey.
apiary.example: One of the best parts of having a beekeeper for a sister-in-law is getting fresh jars of local honey from the family apiary.

matriculate.gloss:  verb To matriculate is to enroll or be enrolled as a student, especially at a college or university.
matriculate.example: She matriculated at the Rhode Island School of Design and began classes in the fall. // A spokesperson for the college said the school is expected to matriculate approximately 1,000 students for the fall semester.
